title_original: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth Review: David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino Bring the Best from Each Other
excerpt_original: Does a director’s reputation deflate with one misfire or wobble through years of accumulated bad taste? David Fincher has managed both. It’s not that he ever maintained a perfect track record—just ask him how inauspiciously the feature-filmmaking career began—but until 2020,…

blocks.text: Does a director’s reputation deflate with one misfire or wobble through years of accumulated bad taste? David Fincher has managed both. It’s not that he ever maintained a perfect track record—just ask him how inauspiciously the feature-filmmaking career began—but until 2020, Fincher never delivered anything so vexing as Mank , which collates insistent criticism, overeager defenses, and derisive chuckles in one word. I don’t know if what I wrote off the back of a single impatient viewing captures how I’d feel now; certainly we like to think our taste evolves some way or another over six years. Yet Mank felt so off from Fincher’s uber-exact formulae that it’s made most forget The Killer —not for nothing about trying to undo a screw-up, and really quite thorough in its explication of such— was precisely the dense confectionery that only he offers within modern American cinema.

People have found reasons to be mad at Quentin Tarantino since 1992, each release offering an ostensibly fresh excuse to trot out personal grievances like everyone’s individual parade float. He also hasn’t produced a single movie since 2019, and the intervening years—despite his protests to the contrary—really suggest the desire to do anything (write a novel and book of criticism, write and direct a play, start a podcast, choose to live in Israel) than make a self-imposed final film. Cinema culture having just so many people it can focus on at any given time and even fewer original thoughts at its disposal, familiar arguments about the apparently inextricable man and work (plagiarism, sexism, Bruce Lee, really just pick one and run with it) have been recurring in an ever-coarser feedback loop. The feeding process became so starved as to reach hysterics when, last year, he made dismissive (and, yes, mean) comments on a podcast hosted by Bret Easton Ellis, which is like being mad at someone for eating meat while visiting Korea.

Had a collaboration between Fincher and Tarantino arrived ten years prior, it would’ve generated a cottage industry of anticipation and speculation. In 2026 I’ve mostly read complaints around the prospect—some sense of the wrong time for each author’s career, of a ship having sailed.

An encroaching out-of-timeness and spectral irrelevancy plagued Rick Dalton, the movie star whose sole recourse was a stunt double who happened to look, sound, or behave nothing much like him. These feelings were resonant when Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood debuted in 2019, but the years since have exclusively hardened its effects: a film released in the last seasons before COVID (for any of the million things that implies), before the film industry entered crises it’s seemingly never quite escaped, as the public became further and further aware of this medium’s fragility. A sequel-of-sorts from these two arriving in rather limited distribution before entering the Netflix’s content sea is either a sad state of affairs or perfect distillation of where things are. Likely it’s both.

That sense of things not being quite what they were, and what they even are trending towards a dim zero, has metastasized to nearly every scene, often each consecutive second in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth —on a sound-and-image basis a David Fincher film yet dual-functioning as an exhaustive, exhausting cinema-history-of-one encyclopedia that almost makes the Quentin Tarantino credit (screenwriter and narrator both) redundant. Their odd pairing—a digital and streaming partisan whose lone gesture towards cinephilic filmmaking rang false; a physical and theatrical evangelist often accused of only making movies about movies—begins in a delightful mangling. A torrent of grain puts Cliff Booth ’s first seconds in a meta movieland: Fincher so densely saturates the screen with analogue textures that what we’re looking at is a question all its own, and where the A-B rhyming scheme of perverse, verbose dialogue is explicitly Tarantino’s, it’s heard from a faded film soundtrack that renders it near-illegible. The technical perfectionist (who might have done 50 takes of these shots) and dialogue obsessive (who might have fought to retain each line verbatim) let their dual instincts flame out while dazzling for permitting three, four, five layers of sound (movie-within-movie, theater showing movie, booth projecting movie, stage behind screen).

The man operating the projector and running sundry side jobs, each timed to a film reel he knows by heart, is Cliff Booth. He still looks and sounds like Brad Pitt, albeit eight years worse for wear: his established beer-and-pizza diet’s begun showing in his face, forcing one to wonder if all the cracks about Rick Dalton (who’s since relocated to Australia for a TV job) getting fat are a touch of self-reflection. The voice, meantime, is lower and slower, sparking its own questions about a less-flexible range of dialogue structure and delivery—a flaw in Tarantino’s script, a hitch in Pitt’s performance, or something of the strange rut Cliff now finds himself in. But the lack of stunt work has not halted Cliff’s strength; if anything, eight unrecoverable years of life have made him more vicious. The previous film’s rumors of wife-killing and threats of knocked-out teeth have become this film’s early post-murder promise: “Trust me: I’ll be very convincing.”

Where Cliff has found himself engenders, in a father-son dynamic with Peter Weller’s Gus Booth, one of the most unvarnished and nerve-gracing in the cinema of Tarantino, a man who cites his childhood’s rotating cast of father figures as catalyst for cinephilia. Who the primary plot machinations have him meet—Elizabeth DeBicki’s Karen Crosby and Scott Caan’s Charlie Peters—galvanize Tarantino’s love of inter-character play: romantic frankness, sexual tension as he’s never quite traced such (delayed, fulfilled, self-sabotaged), professional one-upsmanship that’s come to supplant a prior friendship’s warmth and camaraderie. And where Cliff Booth has a dry stretch, at least one palpable dead zone in its table-setting of plot—a sturdy pulp excursion nevertheless, with the most unrelenting antagonists in his canon and some who are at least in Fincher’s upper echelon—finally makes way for more play. Until it stops to send one of modern movies’ most-beloved characters into an inexorably terrifying scenario.

For all the speculation this film has sparked, it should’ve been more obvious that David Fincher saw a movie about personal disappointments haunted by the specter of gnarly violence and sought to extract from its sequel’s 230-page script everything that would lean into them harder. All chaos in Cliff Booth either moves faster—much faster—or takes Hollywood ’s slow dread one step further. Its predecessor’s climax was lent its danger less from historic precedent (not that this hurt) but for Susan Atkins’ threats of savagery (“I say we cut their cocks off and make them eat it”) presenting a check Tarantino has been known to cash. Its primary danger established twice over, Cliff Booth orients a climax that’s a functionally perfect dramatic scenario and ideal meeting of these two artists: several immediately succeeding sensations across something of a Cielo Drive reiteration that’s altogether tenser, harsher, scarier, more pathos-laden, less resolute, yet finally of a perfect piece with Tarantino’s concept of movie characters stuck in the real world. To say nothing of David Fincher’s perpetual prankster instincts: what I thought was a sudden stop and regrettably pulled punch instead adds him to a list of auteurs who rail against Netflix’s skip-credits button.

The continuity between these films is compelling, odd, of philosophies it’s hard to locate in any other sequel. (Or as a conversation with its author’s novelization that served to recenter its own source.) For consigning the co-lead of an instant classic to a lesser state years hence, Cliff Booth ’s closest comparison—for tone less than form—is Wong Kar-wai’s 2046 . Perhaps it’s more germane to look elsewhere; certainly it’s the lone movie that’s made me think of Bryan Ferry self-covering Roxy Music on a solo record while his band was still in the studio. If the aesthetic leap between 1969 and 1977 is nigh impossible for the modern mind to comprehend when, seven years since Hollywood , few of our own textures have palpably changed, it necessitates in the deliberate tone-down—Robert Richardson’s shimmering film photography to Erik Messerschmidt’s earth-hue digital images—a moment of recalibration. Tarantino has scripted Booth to be stranded by people and in a world of which he was already losing command and—at the risk of placing Cliff Booth as some riposte to cultural conversations around Hollywood , an argument of potentially limited heft—comes across hilariously antagonistic by having a fight with Bruce Lee brought up in a verbal ricochet that Cliff stands in the midst of, avoidantly. A blink-and-miss cameo from one of Hollywood ’s players could be read as too cute by half; per that movie’s ending, it played rather sad once taken from the vantage I suspect he and Fincher wish. Which is likely true of all but a handful of scenes amidst 140 minutes.

“I know better than getting in the way of a good story” is spoken during a sequence that, chronologically, might transpire within a handful of minutes but expands to so many as ten through numerous multi-media digressions. (Watching a seamless-yet-showy transition from TV to film set, it’s unthinkable that these are the same director and cinematographer who, just six years prior, directed a classic Hollywood homage in widescreen out of aversion to the Academy ratio.) Inasmuch as a film with so many on-a-silver-platter satisfactions and only a set of functional issues could be considered challenging, Cliff Booth asks that we locate the pluralities and valences in mild entertainment—their easy pleasures and bad histories, the bonds they form, the thwarted dreams therein.

To what extent this is atomized is anyone’s guess (or projection). Fincher and Tarantino, with their odd misfortune of being the two most-famous and -seen directors of their generation, are surrounded by a surmount of received wisdom that is neither small nor worthy enough to fully address. Still, the notion of either as cold or juvenile rankles further in sight of Cliff Booth . Through a macro lens, all herein—each frivolous-at-first-blush conversation, these myriad expressions of love and rage, a breathtakingly exhaustive late-film photo montage—tells us everyone is running out of time. It’s an assured, mature work that doesn’t forget to have fun, a lark with terrifying contours. What might’ve been Tarantino’s peculiar last movie is Fincher’s best in fifteen-something years. They couldn’t have found each other at a better moment.
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth opens in IMAX on November 25 and streams on Netflix on December 23.
